newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AWB claims A$100 mln sales bonus from market moves.
newsitem.headline: AWB claims A$100 mln sales bonus from market moves.

text.p: The Australian Wheat Board (AWB) said early planning and calculated risk-taking on carryover and shipping capacity had allowed it to realise the full potential of a bumper crop and had produced a A$100 million bonus.
General manager merchandising Ron Storey said that in September and October last year the AWB decided to ship 15 to 20 percent more wheat than ever before, despite exceptionally low carryover stocks.
By the end of March 1997 AWB had shipped 8.5 million tonnes of new season wheat, eclipsing the previous best of 5.7 million tonnes set in 1995/96 by 2.8 million tonnes, or 50 percent.
That year, 1995/96, was also at the time a record year, beating the previous best shipment of 4.8 million tonnes in 1983/84.
The AWB's marketers are also having their most successful year ever, Storey said.
By the end of March they had priced 14 million of the 20 million tonnes of export wheat, far ahead of expectations in the trade, he said.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture was predicting in January that on its October-September operating year, Australia would export 13.5 million tonnes and carry 6.5 million tonnes into next season.
The actual carryout for the AWB at September 30 was expected to be less than 2.5 million tonnes, Storey said.
"The prospect of a record crop meant extra risks needed to be taken," he said.

"We had to ensure carryout was at an all-time low and we had a deliberate strategy to run our stocks to bare bones. We also pre-committed as much of the crop before it arrived in very early sales slots, assuming shipping levels well above our previous best.
The minimal carryover made the shipping target even more ambitious," he said.

"It was no good putting our reputation with customers at risk by not performing so we had to work out ways to exceed the best ever performances consistently. The result is that we have been able to take advantage of sales opportunities that have
come up," he said.
The AWB would be about four million tonnes ahead of its previous best shipping programme by the end of April, he said.
Shipping before the new U.S. crop allows the AWB to take advantage of better prices and saves on storage and finance costs, adding value to the crop.
The four million tonne first quarter advantage was worth about A$25 a tonne, converting to a straight A$100 million extra for growers, he said.
The AWB was confident its carryout at December 1 would be only about one million tonnes, he said.

"Given that we have the largest single export available in the history of the Australian wheat industry, the achievement means we aren't starting behind scratch next year and makes this year's performance even more valuable," he said.
AWB was also in a strong position for the second half of 1997, Storey said.
The 1997 crop would be smaller than the record 23.0 million tonnes crop of 1996 but was expected to be still large, he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
